beats.text: It took a long time, too long for anyone in a hurry.
In 1978, an oilman named Bill Clements became the first Republican governor
of Texas in more than 100 years.
He won by less than one percentage *point*.
In 1980, Ronald Reagan carried Texas, so did every Republican
presidential candidate after him.
And conservative Democrats started *switching* parties.
A congressman named Phil Gramm switched in 1983.
A young legislator named Rick Perry switched in 1989.
In 1994, George W. Bush beat the popular Democratic Governor Ann Richards.
That same year, Democrats won their last statewide races in Texas for 32 years.
In 2002, Republicans won the Texas House for the first time since Reconstruction.
The Dial was finally, completely *red*.
So why did Texas turn red?
It depends on who you ask.
Republicans and many conservatives say Texas didn't really change,
the national Democratic Party did.
It moved left on taxes, guns, abortion, and the role of government,
while Texans stayed where they were.
Add oil money, booming suburbs, and millions of newcomers from
other states who wanted low taxes, and you get a Republican Texas.
Critics, and many historians of the South, say race was at the heart of it.
The switch picked up speed right after the civil rights laws,
and since then, they argue, district maps and voting rules have
helped lock in Republican power.
Most historians would say it was some of both, and that it happened slowly,
over 30 years, not in one night.
